transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. I just... I can’t shake this feeling that I’ve messed everything up at work and that everyone can see how worthless I am, like it’s all being recorded as proof against me. It has gotten to the point where I feel so ashamed and overwhelmed that I can barely function.

When you feel that you are being recorded, do you believe this is literally happening through hidden devices or cameras, or does it feel more like a metaphor for your intense feelings of shame and self-criticism?

It feels completely literal and real to me, not like a metaphor at all; I genuinely believe my mistakes are being recorded on a hidden server to prove I'm incompetent and dangerous. I even hear a low, male voice whispering that they have it all on camera, which makes me look around the room for hidden speakers because it sounds so real.
How long have you been experiencing these specific beliefs about being recorded and hearing this voice, and have you had any periods in the past where you felt completely free of these thoughts?

This has been going on for about four months, starting right after a big cheating investigation at work. I never had these thoughts or heard that voice before I fell into this deep depression. On the rare days when my mood lightens up a bit, the voice and the feeling of being watched also seem to fade into the background.
Do you experience these feelings of being watched and the voices only when your mood is at its absolute lowest, or do they persist even when you feel slightly better?

They really only happen when my mood is at its absolute lowest. On the rare days when this heavy depression lifts even slightly, the whispering and the feeling of being watched fade away too. I never experienced any of this before I fell into this deep, dark state.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms (delusions of being recorded and auditory hallucinations) are clearly mood-congruent and occur exclusively within the context of a severe depressive episode. The patient reports that these psychotic features remit when the mood improves, which strongly supports a diagnosis of severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms rather than a primary psychotic disorder like schizophrenia or a delusional disorder.
